title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models

details.title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models
details.abstract: What does it mean for an AI to understand space? 🌌 Not just to recognize what is in front of it, but to build an internal world: where things are, how they relate, and how that world changes when the viewpoint changes. We found evidence that multimodal models have already begun to build such a world inside themselves. We call it S-Space 🧠 — an internal spatial workspace that can be read, manipulated, and transformed during reasoning. A glimpse into how AI may learn not just to see the physical world, but to reconstruct and reason within it. ✨

title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control

details.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
details.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs

details.title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs
details.abstract: We're excited to share our latest work, VisionWeave! As multimodal models move toward long-horizon interaction with both digital and real-world environments, visual token efficiency has become a critical bottleneck for practical deployment. We argue that the key is to let models natively operate over elastic visual representations — a capability we call VisionWeave. Over the past year, sparse attention has evolved from a post-training trick into a native model capability. We believe visual token efficiency holds the same promise. Building on prior ideas from this line of research, VisionWeave pushes efficiency from a task-specific trick toward a robust, model-native paradigm. Validated on the frontier Qwen3.8-27B: The model adaptively weaves visual representations of mixed granularities conditioned on the input content, enabling adaptive, efficient understanding Extensively evaluated across 8 domain benchmarks × multiple resolution tiers × multiple video frame rates Saves 43.0% of visual tokens on average while retaining 98.9% of native performance Under SGLang deployment: 2.30× throughput and 54.4% lower TTFT Efficiency, robustness, and real-world deployability — all in one native capability. We believe weaving elastic visual representations can become a built-in ability of future models, paving the way for efficient, long-horizon interaction between multimodal foundation models and their visual environments. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07987

title: Here the World in Stereo: Learning Dynamic Spatial Correspondence for Immersive Joint Video-Audio Generation

details.title: Here the World in Stereo: Learning Dynamic Spatial Correspondence for Immersive Joint Video-Audio Generation
details.abstract: Recent joint video-audio generation models have achieved strong semantic correspondence and temporal synchronization. However, applications such as AR/VR and interactive gaming further require stereo audio to provide an immersive sense, which remains largely overlooked. Effective stereo audio requires the perceived sound location to evolve consistently with the motion of its corresponding visual source. We refer to this property as Dynamic Spatial Correspondence and propose StereoBind, a framework that binds visual source motion to stereo sound generation. StereoBind uses motion tracks to coordinate visual motion and stereo audio through three complementary mechanisms. Visual Motion Binding establishes source-aware audiovisual correspondence, the Spatial Track Encoder captures absolute source positions, and Residual Track RoPE models relative motion. For supervision and evaluation, we construct StereoWorld-29K, a large-scale stereo audio-video dataset with paired motion tracks, and StereoWorldBench for measuring audiovisual spatial consistency. Experiments show that StereoBind substantially improves spatial alignment in stereo audio generation over existing models while preserving overall audiovisual quality.

WorkDemo-350 contains 350 human GUI demonstrations, checked for completeness and successful task execution. Agentic skill induction examines demonstration evidence on demand to extract workflow rules, dependencies between steps, and criteria for checking completion. Across four execution models, Work2Skill improves mean scores over each model’s corresponding No Skill baseline by: +4.67 to +10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action. +3.11 to +7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates among the compared skill-induction methods. We’d love to hear your thoughts on learning reusable agent skills from human workflows. Happy to discuss the method and experiments!

title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition

details.title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition
details.abstract: In Learning Beyond Gradients, Jiayi Weng (@trinkle23897) discusses Heuristic Learning (HL): an agent acts as the learner, using experience and feedback to directly improve executable structures such as programs. Looking back, isn't every contestant's development process a form of heuristic learning? Understand the rules, write a strategy, test it, and revisit losses. Find a weakness and turn an insight into code. The contestant is the learning engine, converting experience into a stronger program. Following this idea, we replace the human learning engine with an AI agent and formalize HL in adversarial tasks as Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL). The foundation model's weights stay fixed. The agent understands the rules, selects opponents, analyzes feedback, and generates and maintains the game-playing agent that enters each match. Agents could test more persistently, organize replays systematically, and draw inspiration from different players. But whether these advantages lead to victories requires actual competition. To investigate, we built AAArena, drawing on the contest's archives to collect 12 historical competition games and 1,920 human-written program submissions. Agents compete for leaderboard positions through the same basic process as human players: read the rules, play matches, and improve the code. To give different agents a common evaluation budget, each game provides 128 units for small matches and 16 evaluations against the full opponent pool. Small matches let the agent select opponents, compete, and inspect replays. Full evaluations return the current strategy's Elo rating and rank. Agents decide when to learn and when to submit; comparisons use their best official result achieved within the budget. Across seven AI models and their runtime configurations, Opus5.5 with Claude Code earned six gold medals. No tested configuration topped the other six leaderboards. Agents can already match strong human competitors in some games; the remaining games reveal where their abilities fall short.

title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers

details.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
details.abstract: TL;DR: Can a plain Transformer generate high-quality images directly in pixel space, with no VAE and no specialized pixel decoder? We show that it can, provided its internal representation is both properly formed and actively exploited . 🔍 Two insights Better representations ≠ better generation. REPA-style alignment improves semantics at the aligned layer, but the gain fades in later layers and does not improve final FID. Pixel decoders mostly shift work around. PixelDiT, DiP, and DeCo change how semantic and spatial modeling is split between encoder and decoder, but they do not yield representations better suited to generation. 💡 Representation Guidance (RG) A low-dimensional bottleneck packs generation-relevant information into a compact implicit latent. The decoder's velocity with vs. without the representation gives an offset, which we use to modify the flow-matching target : v_RG = v + (s-1)·sg(Δv_rep) . This forces the decoder to depend on the representation, and in turn shapes the encoder toward what synthesis needs. This works like self-distillation in SSL: the representation is bootstrapped from the model's own predictions. 📈 Results ImageNet 256: FID 1.55 (RG-XL/16, 725M). RG-L/16 with only 459M params beats much larger pixel DiTs, including the 2B JiT-G. 4× faster convergence : RG-B reaches JiT-B's 600-epoch FID in 150 epochs. ImageNet 512: FID 1.74 . Text-to-image: GenEval 0.89 / DPG-Bench 87.1 . 🌐 Project: https://pan-zihao.github.io/Representation-Guidance/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/Pan-Zihao/Representation-Guidance

details.abstract: DCOCO makes parallel speculative decoding faster by restoring dependencies that diffusion-based drafters lose when predicting multiple future tokens simultaneously. Instead of committing to one token per position, it scores multiple candidates using their contextual compatibility and selects a better draft, all while preserving parallelism. title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning

details.title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: Can strong process reward models emerge from outcome-only reinforcement learning? We introduce TIPS (Thinking-Induced Process Supervision), a simple framework that trains generative PRMs using only outcome-level correctness rewards, without human step annotations, Monte Carlo rollouts, or explicit process supervision. By rewarding accurate outcome judgments, TIPS implicitly encourages models to verify intermediate reasoning steps. With just 3.2K outcome-labeled trajectories, TIPS-Qwen3-4B-Thinking achieves 85.2 F1 on ProcessBench, outperforming all evaluated trained PRMs and strong proprietary LLM judges, including GPT-5.4-Instruct and Claude-4.7-Opus. Our results suggest that process supervision can emerge from outcome-only RL, offering a scalable and cost-effective path toward stronger reasoning verification. Code: https://github.com/RUCBM/TIPS

title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents

details.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
details.abstract: Hi everyone👋 Static coding benchmarks don't last long. Their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents saturate them. In SWE-Duel, we try a different approach: coding agents create tasks for each other at evaluation time, so there's nothing to leak in advance, and the difficulty grows with the agents themselves. How it works: two agents take turns as Red and Blue on a real repository. Red adds a new feature, then hides a subtle bug in it, with sealed tests that trigger the bug. The task only counts if a fresh session of the same agent can fix the bug blind, so there are no unsolvable tasks. Blue reviews the PR without being told there's a bug. It wins only if its revision passes the feature tests, the existing tests, and the hidden bug tests. Then they swap roles. We ran 1,500 turns with 11 model-harness pairs on 15 repos in 5 languages. A few findings: GPT-5.5 + Codex CLI ranks 1st as the strongest solver, fixing 98.3% of the bugs it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 + mini-swe-agent ranks 2nd as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Within one model family, tasks written by the newest version beat a fixed reference solver far more often than those from older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%). This suggests task difficulty scales with the agents' own ability. Happy to answer any questions!

title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression

details.title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression
details.abstract: The interesting idea here is that a reward model doesn’t need to spell out every evaluation step to make a good judgment. LatentGRM compresses rubric-based reasoning into continuous latent states, keeping judgment accuracy competitive while cutting inference time by roughly 6–7× in the reported 8B experiments at vote@5. The rubric interventions are especially interesting: changing evaluation criteria changes the resulting preferences, suggesting that the latent trajectories retain criterion-specific information. There’s also an offline interpreter that recovers evaluation text from teacher-derived trajectories. It’s a promising way to make reasoning-heavy judges cheaper, with some visibility into what survives compression.

title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks

details.title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks
details.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench .

title: DataVista: Diagnosing Multimodal LLMs on Data Video Understanding

details.title: DataVista: Diagnosing Multimodal LLMs on Data Video Understanding
details.abstract: Data video is a media form that integrates data visualization with video narrative, widely adopted in news reporting and business analysis. Compared with general video understanding, data video understanding places greater emphasis on accurately reading data from animated charts, integrating evidence across charts and time, and understanding how narrative organization and visual design communicate information. Yet existing benchmarks target either general videos or static charts, and data video understanding has not been systematically evaluated. We present DataVista, the first benchmark for data video understanding, containing 961 real-world data videos and 6,775 evaluation questions organized under a three-level progressive capability framework (data perception, temporal reasoning, narrative understanding) with 10 fine-grained question types across five topic domains. Systematic evaluation of 19 mainstream MLLMs shows that the best-performing model, Gemini-3.1-Pro, achieves 70.0% overall accuracy, still far below human expert performance, with models performing worst on Causal Reasoning and Narrative Structure. Increasing frame counts and adding subtitles mainly benefit data perception and temporal reasoning, with limited gains in narrative understanding. Further analysis of model responses identifies typical failure modes in chart reading, evidence judgment, and instruction understanding. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DataVista .

details.title: From Given to Gathered Evidence: Agentic Learning for Longitudinal Medical Reasoning

Existing medical AI benchmarks primarily evaluate reasoning over preselected information, overlooking the ability to autonomously gather, compare, and synthesize evidence across clinical records and longitudinal imaging. We introduce CASE (Clinical Agents for Seeking Evidence) , shifting medical AI from passive question answering to active, evidence-grounded clinical investigation . Key Contributions Longitudinal Multimodal Benchmark. A UK Biobank-based benchmark comprising 50,401 clinical questions from 4,739 participants , integrating clinical records and multi-sequence MRI across baseline and follow-up visits. Autonomous Evidence-Seeking Agents. A role-conditioned, multi-tool framework enabling compact vision-language models to autonomously select visits, modalities, anatomical structures, image slices, and specialist tools for evidence collection and cross-visit reasoning. Beyond Teacher Imitation. An agentic post-training framework integrating Agentic RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), and RLAIF to improve evidence-to-conclusion reasoning while preserving autonomous tool-use decisions.

We study whether scaling human visual-tactile data benefits both perception and robot manipulation: Cross-sensor contact prediction: zero-shot contact IoU on an unseen tactile sensor improves from 0.134 to 0.383 compared with training on prior tactile data. Action recognition: TouchScale pretraining achieves the highest accuracy on three benchmarks among the visual-tactile datasets compared. Robot manipulation: visual-tactile mid-training improves average real-world success from 22.5% to 57.5% across four contact-rich tasks. With sensing and collection held fixed, larger TouchScale training subsets generally improve tactile prediction and robot success. title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution

details.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
details.abstract: We introduce Video-RSI , a framework for recursive self-improvement of video understanding agents through harness evolution. Instead of updating model weights, Video-RSI enables the agent to revisit the original training videos used for evolution, gather additional visual, transcript, and OCR evidence, and test competing explanations for its failures. Evidence-supported diagnoses are then translated into reusable changes to the agent’s prompts, tools, memory, and execution logic. Video-RSI uses a cost-aware selection process to retain revisions based on both answer accuracy and visual processing cost. Across the evaluated video understanding benchmarks, the evolved harness improves accuracy while processing fewer frames, yielding competitive accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. We release the inference and evaluation code, the initial and final harnesses, and the implementation of the harness-evolution workflow. We welcome feedback and discussion from the community.

title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: Can on-policy distillation transfer an improvement without requiring a stronger teacher? In Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation, we study how the log-probability difference between a proxy expert and a proxy reference can guide a target model on its own rollouts. Our any-to-any OPD formulation treats this difference as an implicit reward and recovers conventional OPD as a special case. We find that differences created by RL or SFT transfer more reliably than those arising from model scale alone. The expert supplies the capability, the reference isolates the part to transfer, and the target must be able to learn and generalize the resulting update. These findings offer practical guidance for choosing source pairs and targets—including cases where changing the reference turns a failed transfer into a successful one. Code: https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/A2-OPD

title: When Do Biological Reasoning Models Use Their Biological Inputs?

details.title: When Do Biological Reasoning Models Use Their Biological Inputs?
details.abstract: Do biological reasoning models actually use the biological inputs they receive? We investigate this question across six models spanning DNA, protein, and single-cell tasks, using input perturbations, evidence conflicts, linear probes, and reasoning-trace analyses. We find that benchmark accuracy alone can obscure whether a model relies on biological sequence or cell representations: BioReason and BioReason-Pro often favor accompanying biological text, while other evaluated models show meaningful dependence on their biological inputs. We also find that higher accuracy after post-training does not necessarily mean greater use of biological evidence.

details.abstract: This paper investigates when communication emerges in evolutionary robotics and how its emergence depends on the value of information available to autonomous agents. Using evolved e-puck robots reconstructed in PyBullet and validated against Webots, we show that referential communication naturally appears when it provides a measurable advantage and tends to disappear when equivalent information is directly available. The study also examines how innate action-selection mechanisms influence the evolution of communication, providing evidence that some forms of built-in behavioral scaffolding can hinder performance in social tasks.

title: QuantMLA: Function-Aligned Dual-Path Quantization for Low-Bit MLA KV Caching

details.title: QuantMLA: Function-Aligned Dual-Path Quantization for Low-Bit MLA KV Caching
details.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) enables expressive multi-head attention with compact caches for its content and decoupled RoPE paths, yet cache memory still scales linearly with context length and batch size. In this work, we establish a systematic model of MLA's dual-path quantization errors, characterizing their distinct effects on attention-output distortion and explaining the pronounced amplification of RoPE-path errors. Guided by this analysis, we introduce QuantMLA, a function-aligned framework for low-bit dual-path quantization. We derive path-specific transformation spaces that preserve full-precision computation while remaining fully fusible into model parameters offline, eliminating online transformation overhead. Within these spaces, QuantMLA learns path-specific transformations with function-aligned objectives: attention-output reconstruction captures the content path's coupled matching and aggregation errors, while positional QK reconstruction preserves the RoPE-induced component of the attention logits and admits a theoretical bound on output distortion. Across four MLA model families, QuantMLA enables, to our knowledge, the first reported joint INT4 caching of the content and RoPE caches with minimal accuracy degradation. Further compressing the content cache to INT2 while retaining the RoPE key cache at INT4 maintains competitive performance on challenging reasoning and code benchmarks. We develop a native low-bit MLA attention kernel that integrates unpacking and dequantization directly into attention computation. The physical cache layout provides 3.59x compression at 128K context, while a cache-pressure serving workload achieves 5.168x higher whole-job output throughput than BF16. The code will be released upon acceptance.

title: MAMHOI: Factorizing Scene-Aware Human-Object Interaction through Affordances

details.title: MAMHOI: Factorizing Scene-Aware Human-Object Interaction through Affordances
details.abstract: We introduce MAMHOI, a framework for generating scene-aware human–object interactions in complex 3D environments. Our key observation is that this task requires two complementary capabilities: understanding where an interaction can be feasibly performed within a scene and synthesizing how the human and object should move together. However, paired human–object–scene motion data providing both forms of supervision remains scarce. MAMHOI addresses this challenge by factorizing scene-aware HOI generation through motion affordances. A scene-conditioned model learns to predict task-relevant affordances from diverse indoor human–scene interaction data, while an affordance-conditioned generative model learns coordinated human–object dynamics from scene-free HOI data. The predicted affordance provides a shared representation that connects scene understanding with interaction synthesis. This factorization allows MAMHOI to adapt learned human–object interactions to complex environments without requiring paired human–object–scene training data. Our experiments show that the resulting motions better respect scene geometry, substantially reduce object–scene penetration, and preserve the quality of human–object interactions. We welcome comments, questions, and feedback from the community!

Verify: Evaluate the answer using five complementary verification perspectives. Decide: Accept reliable answers, or rethink using verification feedback and interaction history. Answering and verification use the same backbone VLM, without an external judge during inference. 📊 Main results Evaluation covers five benchmarks and three VLM backbones . Average accuracy across the five benchmarks improves as follows: Backbone Baseline MOTIVE Gain Qwen2.5-VL-3B 55.11% 63.13% +8.02 pp Qwen2.5-VL-7B 60.49% 68.63% +8.14 pp pp = percentage points. MOTIVE also reduces the average number of answer-generation turns compared with conventional self-verification. 💡 What motivates this approach? Verifier capability matters. Stronger external judges improve final-answer accuracy in our preliminary analysis, motivating the development of stronger self-verification. Prompt choice matters. No single verification prompt consistently performs best across tasks. This motivates combining complementary verification perspectives.

title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

details.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
details.abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) , an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.

title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning

details.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
details.abstract: With SpatialASM, we explore whether LVLMs can go beyond passively observing the given images and instead actively reason by planning task-relevant viewpoints and mentally imagining what should be visible from them. We introduce Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM) and build a scalable training framework around it. SpatialASM uses an allocentric novel-view generator as training-time scaffolding to synthesize explicit plan-imagine-reason trajectories and automatically verifiable perspective-taking tasks. In this way, models learn both when to seek missing spatial evidence and how to reconstruct it internally without requiring additional views or a renderer at inference time. This is our attempt to bring a more human-like form of active spatial exploration into LVLMs and alleviate the scarcity of high-quality spatial reasoning supervision. Across four LVLM backbones and seven spatial benchmarks, SpatialASM improves spatial reasoning performance while preserving general visual capabilities. We’d love to hear your thoughts and feedback!

title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method

details.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) has largely focused on a single agent following a single instruction, yet many real-world applications require teams of robots to tackle tasks beyond the capabilities of any individual agent. We present Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation, the first systematic formalization of multi-agent VLN as a constrained coordination problem: each mission consists of subtasks carrying dependency and resource constraints (presence locks and holding chains). MAVLN is a benchmark built with a verified four-stage crafting pipeline. It contains 11,724 episodes across 145 HM3D scenes, with teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, and comes with constraint-aware metrics. TRISS is a coordination-ready navigation system. It couples an LLM-based subtask scheduler, a shared topological memory that turns each agent's exploration into team knowledge, and a conflict-aware execution mechanism that realizes simultaneous intentions as collision-free routes. Extensive experiments establish TRISS as a comprehensive baseline and reveal substantial room for improvement across scheduling, navigation, and execution.

title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training

details.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
details.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

These capabilities provide a foundation for organizations deploying LLMs in high-value real-world scenarios, including complex decision-making, long-term planning and autonomous agent execution. Vela explores anonymized user behavior as supervision to develop these capabilities and strengthen broader LLM intelligence . details.title: Scoring Higher, Answering Worse: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL via Protocol-Level Rubrics
details.abstract: Can an AI get a better score by giving a worse answer? Surprisingly, yes. Imagine asking whether to call 911—and getting 2,000+ characters of explanation before the model tells you to call. The answer checks plenty of boxes, but misses what matters: getting the urgent advice to you immediately. We found that rubric-based RL can encourage this behavior. When checklist scores simply add up, models can earn points for extra details that compensate for a critical mistake. ProRubric changes how those points are earned. Related requirements must pass together, and a critical failure wipes out the group’s credit. On Qwen3-4B, this improves appropriateness by 10.8 points over standard Rubric-RL without sacrificing rubric coverage. The takeaway: better checklists are only half the story—how we score them matters too.

title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization

details.title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
details.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) builds a teacher from the model itself by giving it privileged information (PI) the student can't see. We find PI often pushes the teacher toward shortcut answers, suppressing re-checking tokens like "Wait" and "However" and collapsing the student's token entropy (near 0 in some runs). The model stops thinking, and downstream accuracy drops. VRSD is a simple fix: we add a training-only system prompt to the teacher, asking it to verify intermediate steps, consider alternative reasoning paths, and revisit earlier judgments. The student never sees this prompt. We model the prompt as attenuating the PI-induced log-prob shift and derive conditions under which teacher entropy is preserved. Across 3 models × 4 tasks (Grading, Chemistry, Text-to-SQL, Python): Pass@1 beats OPSD in 11/12 settings (+3.9 pp avg) Maj@16 never below OPSD; Worst@16 also improves Entropy recovers (e.g., SQL: 0.03 → 0.54) More faithful reasoning: misleading-reasoning rate 3.0% → 1.6% Code: https://github.com/lijiazheng99/VRSD

title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter

details.title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
details.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes.

details.title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
details.abstract: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body.

details.title: Fish Audio Drama 3 Technical Report
details.abstract: We introduce Fish Audio Drama 3, an open-source speech generation model that turns text into directed performances, built on a 35B-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone that activates 3B parameters per token. It clones voices from multiple references, follows natural-language direction, revises a take when the next turn gives a note, voices multi-character scenes, edits existing speech by infilling, and synthesizes long-form and streaming audio. Multi-turn revision, scene dubbing, editing by infilling, and streaming text input are new in Drama 3, all in one model. Drama 3 pairs the hybrid linear-attention backbone with a new codebook multi-token-prediction audio decoder that predicts the acoustic codebooks of each frame in dedicated layers that attend over the entire sequence. The model is trained with a three-stage pre-training recipe, instruction fine-tuning, and large-batch reinforcement learning whose only reward is a single learned model of human preference. Its inference engine decodes a single stream at 271 frames per second on one H200, against 177 for Fish Audio S2, although Drama 3 has more than seven times as many parameters. The model weights are available on GitHub ( https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech ) and Hugging Face (( https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3 ), and inference is available through SGLang-Omni ( https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni ). title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces

details.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
details.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce Panini-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate Panini-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven baseline implementations using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. Panini-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks, with strong gains on harder questions. On BrowseComp-Plus, Panini-DR achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best baseline by 16.0 percentage points, at higher inference cost. Its advantage is strongest on harder investigations, correctly answering 26 of 50 hard questions—nearly twice as many as the next-best baseline. Our ablation studies further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does verification combined with evidence checks. To assess whether correct answers are supported by the research performed, we also analyze the evidence retained by each system. Panini-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how systems compare and further strengthens Panini-DR's advantage over existing approaches.

title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges

details.title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges
details.abstract: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher’s outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.

We introduce LongR , an RL framework that teaches LLMs to “Think-and-Read” —interleaving reasoning with document consultation, guided by more than just final-answer correctness. Our key idea is a dense contextual reward based on relative information gain , encouraging models to extract informative, document-grounded evidence without evidence annotations or rigid document chunking. A progressive curriculum helps this behavior emerge through RL, without handcrafted long-context reasoning demonstrations. arXiv 📈 On LongBench v2, LongR improves Qwen3-4B by 9.79 percentage points over SFT and 5.03 points over outcome-only DAPO , alongside improvements on RULER and InfiniteBench. The takeaway: better long-context reasoning is not just about processing more tokens—it is about learning to use the evidence within them. arXiv We’d love to hear your thoughts! 🚀

details.abstract: Reusable skills improve multimodal agents without updating model weights, but their effectiveness depends on both the evidence presented and the procedure used to read it. We introduce ViewCraft, which jointly evolves an executable evidence interface and its reading procedure. The interface selects, transforms, and organizes observations; the reader interprets the resulting views. Failure traces guide revisions, replay and paired evaluation retain useful changes, and interface projection recovers visual edits from eligible rejected joint proposals. Across eight benchmarks, ViewCraft improves over direct execution by an average of 6.1 points in task score, with gains on every benchmark. The advantage persists at a matched input-token budget. On all five multi-source tasks, the learned interface uses 8%-15% fewer input tokens than initial skill. The learned skills also transfer across executors and outperform direct execution in every evaluated transfer, supporting evidence construction and reading as a coupled, reusable skill.

title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems

details.title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems
details.abstract: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also introduce WebSim and the PsyBer Benchmark, which encompass multimodal scenarios and seven recommender backbones. Our framework evaluates behavioral fidelity, latent-state consistency, robustness, and responses to social-cue perturbations. On the tested horizons, PsyBer-Agent shows lower behavioral discrepancy than the prompt-only simulators while maintaining stable performance under large-scale concurrent simulation for up to 5M queued simulation tasks under bounded concurrency.

With Qwen3-0.6B steering Qwen3-32B, DoubtLess removes 31% of the thinking tokens on seven math, science and coding benchmarks with unchanged accuracy, more than five inference-time baselines. It also cuts the thinking of a self-debugging coding agent by 20%, removes about three times as much as a concise prompt on EXAONE-4.0 and Granite-4.2, and further shortens a model already trained for brevity. The small model adds only about 4% to the FLOPs. Code (vLLM): https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess

Our key observation is that spatial aggregation and temporal correction in causal 3D convolutions respond differently to compression. LightVAE keeps the spatial component dense, applies low-rank compression to temporal correction, and combines block pruning with probe-guided quality recovery—all while preserving the original latent interface. Across Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and MiniMax-H3, it offers a high-fidelity configuration close to the original VAE and a separate faster configuration that reaches 4.2× the original Wan2.1 decoding throughput on RTX 5090. details.title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
details.abstract: Can AI models really replace human survey respondents? We evaluated 47 generative LLMs and 14 decision models against real human survey data, looking beyond plausible answers to psychometric validity. A few interesting findings: Newer doesn't mean better: In 5 out of 10 model families, the latest release performed worse than an earlier version. Probability distributions aren't enough: Decision models capture population-level response distributions surprisingly well, but struggle to reproduce human correlation patterns and individual responses. Simple statistical baselines remain competitive: Even the best LLMs couldn't clearly outperform a Gaussian copula trained on real survey data. The takeaway: Generating believable survey responses is not the same as generating psychometrically valid synthetic respondents. Curious to hear what others think: What evidence would convince you that synthetic respondents are reliable enough for real research?

title: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery

details.title: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery
details.abstract: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery Test-time RL lets an LLM actually learn from its own attempts on a discovery problem, but reward-only updates tend to collapse onto early high-reward trajectories and kill off directions that look bad now but could pay off later. CURIO adds a curiosity signal to test-time RL : 🧠 Intrinsic Curiosity World Model (ICWM): learns transitions in the policy’s own hidden-state space and gives prediction-error bonuses to sampled tokens outside the policy’s top-k, rewarding genuinely novel reasoning instead of random noise. ⚖️ Stable integration: epoch-wise normalization and an annealed curiosity weight keep the bonus as a complement to task reward, so it doesn’t override it. Results (Qwen3-8B to 235B) : 📐 Beats a matched task-only RL baseline on 5 of 6 math discovery objectives, and matches the best reported result on Circle Packing 🧬 Improves single-cell denoising Score and MSE on both held-out corpora at every scale tested 📈 Up to +18.3% on Hadamard and +10.8% on denoising Score 🌱 Generated programs are measurably more structurally diverse

title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer

details.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
details.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present ShellElastic, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce $\mu$-Elastic, an extension of maximal update parameterization ($\mu$P) to ShellElastic and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously ($\mu$-Internal), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets ($\mu$-Transfer). A single ShellElastic run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.

title: Beyond Prompt Count: How Data Shapes Transfer in On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Beyond Prompt Count: How Data Shapes Transfer in On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: We study how prompt count, source, and selection shape transfer in on-policy distillation (OPD). One motivating result: using “What is 1+1?” as the only training prompt raises Qwen3-4B’s math score from 15.47% to 47.93%, close to the teacher’s 48.33%. This still involves repeated student rollouts and teacher supervision—not a single training update. But prompt efficiency does not imply prompt interchangeability. Our main findings: • Prompt utility depends on the teacher–student pair and target task. Changing only the teacher can reverse the relative effectiveness of math and code prompts. • Teacher-aligned prediction changes can emerge through very different parameter updates. • We probe failure and recovery at the representation level. Hidden-state interventions partially improve a degraded model on a small probe. In a separate experiment, continued OPD on effective prompts restores code performance from 50.03% to 63.16%, without retracing a successful run’s parameter path. • Uniform random sampling remains competitive. Targeted selection—including semantic diversity, difficulty, response length, teacher–student disagreement, and gradient-based selection—does not consistently improve transfer in our experiments. Filtering out a source that performs poorly alone also gives no consistent gain. Have you observed similar sensitivity to prompt choice in your own OPD experiments? Happy to discuss the results and implementation!

title: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling

details.title: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling
details.abstract: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling Video world models repeatedly reuse past observations, but dynamic memories such as 4DGS re-render RGB and re-encode it into conditions for every request. 4LC encodes observations once: features from multiple visual encoders (FLUX.2 VAE, DINOv2, V-JEPA, VGGT) are bound to shared geometry and motion, covering both static and dynamic content. Conditions are then read out directly at any time and viewpoint, with no per-request rendering or re-encoding. ⚡ 68.5× faster condition acquisition and 12.6× lower peak GPU memory (condition share of end-to-end time: 14.9% → 0.25%) 🧩 One model, many tasks without task-specific fine-tuning: camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits and long-term generation, plus image-to-video and video editing 🌐 Project page: https://zgca-hmi-lab.github.io/4LC/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/ZGCA-HMI-Lab/4LC 🤗 Models: https://huggingface.co/jianhuizhang/4LC-Video 🎮 Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/jianhuizhang/4LC-Demo

Video models can produce impressive individual shots, but keeping a whole story consistent is harder: a room should keep its layout when revisited, and different cameras should capture the same event at the same point in time. We introduce ATAS , a world-state-centric framework that gives video agents a shared spatial and temporal reference. 🧠 Two complementary memories : scene memory stores registered static geometry, while event memory stores time-indexed dynamic observations. Each new shot retrieves the evidence it needs. 🎥 Different cameras, one event : agents can revisit earlier locations or replay past events from new viewpoints, querying the same evolving world state. 📊 Evaluated across four video generators : ATAS improves the reported cross-shot consistency measures, with further evaluations covering spatial revisits, event recapture, and human preferences. title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

details.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
details.abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: Developed jointly by JD.com’s OxygenVLM team and Nanjing University, RoadMOPD mitigates learning conflicts among teachers with substantially different response styles and domain expertise, helping a student integrate multiple experts’ capabilities while reducing degradation in individual domains. It brings routed and auxiliary teachers together to evaluate the same student-generated response, using teacher agreement to strengthen jointly supported token-level corrections and attenuate conflicting signals. Preventive gradient projection then suppresses conflicting update components while adaptively preserving the target domain’s learning signal. With Qwen3-4B, RoadMOPD improves both domains over Vanilla MOPD in the high-conflict Math–Medical and Code–Medical settings, boosting average medical accuracy by up to 8.78 percentage points. Benefits also extend to the more compatible Math–Code combination, with improvements across all three domains under joint Math–Code–Medical training. The code is currently undergoing internal company approval for open-source release and is expected to be released within the next 1–2 months.

title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory

details.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
details.abstract: How can multimodal agents remember what they perceive, keep that memory useful as the world changes, and learn to manage it better over time? We are sharing our survey, “Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory.” We organize this growing field around two complementary axes: 🔹 Formation and Representation: How is multimodal information stored—as modality-specific representations, text and structured records, latent or parametric memory, or hybrid representations that preserve links to the original evidence? 🔹 Memory Management: How does memory adapt over time? We distinguish static memory , dynamic memory updated through a stable policy, and self-evolving memory whose management policy improves through experience. A central distinction is that updating memory content and improving the policy that manages memory are different capabilities . Our framework helps clarify this difference and connects memory design to evidence preservation, temporal consistency, and reliable reasoning across long-horizon tasks. The survey also covers memory infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, applications, and open challenges. We hope it serves as a useful guide for researchers and practitioners building multimodal agents. We welcome feedback, discussion, and suggestions for relevant work!

KV4-RL combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection, delivering up to 1.97× rollout speedup and 1.27× end-to-end speedup, with minimal impact on learning performance. title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation

details.title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
details.abstract: Better models. Smarter training data. Different image models struggle with different things. A fixed training set cannot keep up with every model’s evolving strengths and weaknesses. APT makes post-training adaptive. Three agents work together to evaluate the current model, diagnose its failure modes, and generate the training prompts it needs next. After each update, the loop starts again. APT (Agentic Post-Training) turns post-training into a fully automated, evaluation-driven adaptive loop. Given a user-specified evaluation scope, the Evaluation Set Generation Agent constructs a diverse evaluation set consisting of prompt–evaluation rubric pairs; the Diagnosis Agent evaluates the current model on these pairs to identify its strengths and failure modes; and the RL Data Generation Agent adaptively samples next-round training prompts, prioritizing underperforming capabilities. The updated model is then re-evaluated in the next round, allowing the training distribution to continuously adapt to the model's evolving capability profile. This design eliminates the need for manually curated post-training data and makes APT model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution

details.title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution
details.abstract: Can humanoids choose the right tool and then actually use it? We introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark evaluating humanoid tool selection and execution across three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes. We also introduce ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. Evaluating seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals a substantial gap between selecting a suitable tool and successfully completing the task. Additional GR00T N1.7 probes examine generalization to unseen tools and behavior under unrelated instructions. Explore the benchmark and demonstrations on our project page. We welcome feedback from the humanoid learning and tool-use communities!

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios

details.title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
details.abstract: RuleTrek is a multi-domain benchmark for evaluating agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Unlike existing rule-reasoning benchmarks that represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, RuleTrek features complex, multi-file scenarios that require agents to integrate distributed information, identify applicable rules from original rule documents, and correctly apply them to solve tasks in interactive workspaces. RuleTrek evaluates three core capabilities: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs reveal substantial challenges, with E2E scores ranging from 26.97% to 55.29%.

title: τ-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions

details.title: τ-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
details.abstract: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce τ-Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agent–user–environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to τ-Bench and τ-Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, τ-Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision.

title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models

details.title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re sharing RAR (Rate-Adaptive Rollout), a framework for controllable generation rates in interactive world models. Most world models run at a fixed temporal rate, so differences in hardware throughput can unintentionally speed up or slow down the generated world. RAR combines physical-time-aligned Stride-RoPE with synchronized multi-stride training, enabling one model to generate at multiple rates—including unseen intermediate rates—and switch rates mid-rollout without resetting the KV cache. This makes it possible to match the rollout rate to runtime throughput while keeping the world’s physical-time progression consistent. Happy to discuss and hear your feedback!

title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

details.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
details.abstract: Something I keep noticing with AI scientist agents: running more of them in parallel doesn’t make them smarter by default. Mostly they throw away each other’s work. 🧪 Picture a lab where a student has a promising idea but botches the implementation, and the idea gets crossed off. Down the hall, another student’s “failed” project holds the one trick a colleague needed, and nobody ever opens it. Agent swarms run into the same two walls: • A failed experiment doesn’t tell you whether the hypothesis was wrong or the code was • A program with no overall gain can still hold a component another agent needs • So good ideas get abandoned and useful pieces get buried That’s the problem behind our new paper: 🚀 SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm The idea: let the swarm evolve what its agents inherit, not just keep its best scores. • A shared graph records each research state: hypotheses, programs, experimental evidence and open needs • Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents’ feedback to decide whether to revise the hypothesis or repair the program • Complementary Swarm Recombination re-tests kept hypotheses on other agents’ programs (rebase) and merges components that complement each other (crossover) • Recursive Swarm Evolution sends every outcome back into the graph, whether it succeeded, failed or made no gain, so it shapes where the next agent starts Results on 118 scientific coding and ML engineering tasks: 📈 76.2 average on OpenProblems (single-cell), vs 57.2 for human experts and 67.1 for TusoAI 🧬 Matches published SOTA on 44.4% of NatureBench’s 90 tasks, the highest of all compared methods (the best Claude Code setup reaches 35.6%) 🏅 Medals on 81.8% of MLE-Bench Lite competitions, above Arbor and MLEvolve 🔁 About 77% of final best NatureBench programs come from a rebase, a crossover or a feedback-triggered update 🔬 Biologists reproduced two of its programs and used them in follow-up studies of intestinal and splenic immunity I think the next progress in AI for science will come less from adding agents or scaling models, and more from making sure what one agent learns changes where the next one begins. 📝 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20431

title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving

details.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
details.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant.

title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon

details.title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon
details.abstract: Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, tool use, and environment feedback over extended interactions. Learning from sparse outcome rewards requires weighting trajectories of different lengths and updating the policy while rollouts are still being collected. We examine a single-rollout asynchronous recipe combining Muon , token-averaged loss, truncated importance sampling, and auxiliary length and tool-error penalties. Single-rollout sampling allows asynchronous learning without waiting for multiple trajectories for the same issue. We study optimizer choices and recipe components for repository-level issue resolution across two model families. The evaluated training runs show higher training success with the full recipe than with the baselines.

title: Acting Through Registers

details.title: Acting Through Registers
details.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action

details.title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
details.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard.

Meet TextVerifier, our model for detecting subtle errors in generated Chinese text—from missing strokes to malformed components—that OCR and vision-language models can overlook. By representing characters through Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS), TextVerifier learns to assess their visual structure. We also introduce TextRenderBench-ZH, a benchmark with 7,358 individually annotated characters, where TextVerifier achieves 0.844 F1, outperforming OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Beyond evaluation, its scores serve as per-character rewards for Flow-GRPO post-training, helping reduce rendering errors. We’re excited to share this step toward more reliable Chinese text generation—feedback is welcome! 🤗
